**Saint Mary's Church (Leixlip)** (church/chapel, 1780–1820; rated National). Reg. no. 11804017.

Saint Mary’s Church is a fine and well-maintained church of considerable social interest as the ecclesiastical centre for the Church of Ireland population in the locality. Built on the site of, and probably incorporating the fabric of, an earlier medieval church on site, the present building is also of historical and archaeological significance, attesting to the long-standing ecclesiastical presence in the town. Composed of graceful proportions, the church presents a modest appearance, and this is emphasised by the unrefined quality of the rubble stone construction, a feature that represents a traditional method of building in the late eighteenth/early nineteenth century. The exterior of the church remains substantially unaltered and retains important early or original features and materials, including fenestration, timber fittings to the door openings and a slate roof having cast-iron rainwater goods. The interior is similarly intact and incorporates a rare feature in the form of an L-plan gallery to first floor – the construction and support of the gallery is of some technical or engineering merit. Of artistic interest are the various stained glass fittings to the window openings, while the furniture to the chancel/altar is also indicative of the high quality of craftsmanship practised in the locality. The church is set in its own grounds and is surrounded by an attractive graveyard containing cut-stone markers of considerable vintage and artistic merit. Also of significance is the gateway to north, the limestone ashlar piers again attesting to the quality of stone masonry practised in Leixlip, while the gates and railings are fine examples of early wrought iron work. Saint Mary’s Church is an important component of the architectural heritage of Leixlip and is prominently sited just off the line of Main Street. The tower to west, thought to be of medieval origins, is an imposing feature in the town, identifying the church in the locality while providing visual incident to the skyline.

**Church**, Confey. Record KD006-003----.

O'Neill, acknowledging previous studies by O'Keeffe and Manning, argues for three building phases here: he suggests that an original 11th-century, single cell structure was converted into a nave when a chancel and chancel arch were added to its east end in the 12th-century (when it was a possession of the diocese of Glendalough), with the building being enlarged again, probably in the 15th-century, when the nave was extended, to the W. At the north end of a graveyard within a possible field system. A fairly poorly preserved, ivy-clad rectangular structure comprising a well-built nave of roughly dressed and coursed, limestone blocks, to the east end of which a smaller more crudely built chancel was added, but not bonded. The west end of the nave has collapsed, but the inner face of a doorway with segmented arch survives towards the west end of the south wall, together with traces of a possible opposing, but now blocked, doorway in the north wall. The nave is lit by two very narrow windows at the east end of the south wall; the more westerly of which is lintelled, while the easterly one although round-arched has a tympanum-stone under the arch giving a square-headed ope. Two similar, opposing windows occur in the chancel, near the east end of it's north and south walls, and there is a third in the east gable wall of the nave (with a similar tympanum to the one in the south wall) which was blocked-up when the round-headed chancel arch, which springs from rectangular abacuses, was inserted. The chancel was lit by a window in its east gable wall which is robbed-out, and by a narrow flat-headed window, now blocked, at the west end of the south wall. The interior contains 18th/19th century burials marked by headstones, and piles of collapsed building stones.

**Historic town**, Leixlip. Record KD011-004001-.

Located at the confluence of the E-flowing River Liffey and its tributary, the S-flowing Rye Water. According to Bradley et al., the existence of a Scandinavian placename 'Lex-hlaup' / 'salmon leap', suggests a Viking settlement. In the late-12th/early-13th century, Leixlip was also known by the name 'Ernia' or 'Hernie', possibly derived from An Urnaidhe, meaning oratory, which may also indicate the presence of a pre-Norman ecclesiastical site. The earliest definite evidence for settlement occurs in the late-12th century when Adam De Hereford established a castle and borough and granted the church and burgage to St Thomas' Abbey. Subsequently another burgage was given to St. Mary's Abbey in Dublin. The borough was looted and burnt by Edward Bruce's army in 1317, but otherwise seems to have remained relatively undisturbed. A population of 100 was recorded in the census of 1659. The town was confined to a narrow strip of land between the Liffey on the south, a high ridge on the north, and the Rye Water on the west, with the main street running roughly E-west along the centre of this strip of ground. A burgage plot pattern survives on the north and south of Main Street. The settlement included an early castle, a church and graveyard, and a tower house, while archaeological excavation has uncovered medieval deposits to the north of Main Street.

threads.title: Maynooth Castle and the FitzGeralds
threads.spokenNarrative: So: the FitzGeralds. Strongbow – yes, that Strongbow – granted the manor here to Maurice Fitzgerald, and up went a stone castle. Exactly when is a matter of polite disagreement: one official record says probably the late 1180s, another says the early 13th century. Either way, the keep was one of the largest of its kind in Ireland, which tells you something about the family's ambitions. And the ambition paid off. Garret Mór – the 'Great Earl', a nice modest nickname – governed Ireland in the name of the King of England from 1487 to 1513. Under his son, Garret Óg, Maynooth Castle became the centre of political power and culture. Not bad for a plain. Then it all went wrong. The castle fell in the Silken Thomas Rebellion and was badly damaged, and it was dismantled at the time of the 1641 rebellion. Today the State looks after it, and there's an exhibition in the keep. No siege required.

It was built in 1859 in the Gothic Revival style, but the builders kept fabric from an earlier church dated to 1248. Recycling at its finest. The real prize is the tower. It started life around 1450 as part of the Geraldine castle – the FitzGeralds again, they get everywhere – and belonged to the manorial church that went with it. So that tower is really the castle's own church, wearing a 19th-century coat. Up close it has four late medieval windows, a row of narrow slits, and two blocked round-headed openings that were probably doorways to an upper storey of the old church. And the battlements on top? Modern. A little bit of costume jewellery.

threads.title: St Patrick's College
threads.hookSnippet: The idea of a college in Maynooth goes back to 1518, when the ninth Earl of Kildare asked for a licence to found and endow one.
threads.spokenNarrative: The idea of a college in Maynooth goes back to 1518, when the ninth Earl of Kildare asked for a licence to found and endow one. It took a while to happen. St Patrick's College began, from 1796, as one classical house. Then it grew. And grew. By 1815 it had sprouted a great U-shaped range around a courtyard, built to match so neatly that it's hard to tell old from new. Next, Pugin designed the Quadrangle, with a library, kitchens and a chapel – except it was meant to be a full quadrangle, and only a U-shaped range was ever built. A quadrangle with a side missing. Then the showstopper: the College Chapel by J.J. McCarthy, built between 1875 and 1891, with its tower and spire added a few years later. It's been called arguably the finest collegiate chapel in the country. The college even has its own burial ground, for priests who taught or studied here. Loyalty, taken to the very end.

threads.title: What lay beneath the keep
threads.hookSnippet: Castles have a habit of sitting on top of older secrets, and Maynooth's is no exception.
threads.spokenNarrative: Castles have a habit of sitting on top of older secrets, and Maynooth's is no exception. In 1996, archaeologists excavated the entire inside of the keep and found seven main phases of life stacked on one spot – a sort of historical lasagne. At the bottom: part of a prehistoric building, plus a stone axe head and an unfinished macehead. Somebody never got around to finishing that job. Above that, at least two small round houses of post and wattle, probably early medieval, one with a curving wooden stockade. Then the land was farmed, and the furrows ran right over the old houses. The site fell into Norman hands around 1175, and from then comes a mound of sod about a metre high, with a wooden building on top and a stout fence around it. Left behind: an arrowhead, an iron spur and a scabbard chape. Only after all that, probably in the late 1180s, did the stone keep start to rise.

threads.title: The planned town
threads.hookSnippet: Ever get the feeling Maynooth's Main Street is heading somewhere important?
threads.spokenNarrative: Ever get the feeling Maynooth's Main Street is heading somewhere important? It is. It's a planned street, running towards the entrance to the Carton estate. One house on it goes back to the earliest phase of building, around 1750. The gate lodge for Carton Demesne, with its tall red-brick chimneys, went up in 1757. And the Leinster Arms was built in 1777 as a hotel, back in Maynooth's coaching days. In Court House Square there's a limestone sculpture called Axis, from 1993. Its arches are a nod to two buildings that once stood there and vanished: first the market house, then the courthouse. On Pound Lane there's something rarer still: a Catholic church built between 1755 and 1777, one of the few pre-Emancipation churches in County Kildare still in any use. And at the corner of Pound Lane and Mill Street, a curved stone wall from 1821 is a reminder of the old town pound. Presumably the toughest address in town.

threads.title: The Royal Canal and the railway
threads.spokenNarrative: Before motorways, there were canals. This stretch of the Royal Canal was built between 1790 and 1796 to link the east of Ireland with the west, and for some years it helped make Maynooth prosperous. Its bridges are little works of art. Bond Bridge, dated 1795, is a proper hump-backed stone arch, with the towpath running underneath. Mullen Bridge went up the same year, was bypassed in 1995, and still carries a weathered Ordnance Survey benchmark – a tiny mapmaker's mark that has outlived plenty of maps. On the Lyreen River, William Bridge has three arches with triangular cut-waters, and it's from around 1795 too. Clearly a busy year for stonemasons. Then the railway arrived. The signal box at Maynooth station was built in 1847 for the Midland and Great Western Railway: granite downstairs, timber upstairs. It went quiet after 1947, and then in 1981 it was brought back into service. Comebacks don't get much better than that.

threads.title: Laraghbryan: the older story
threads.hookSnippet: Long before the castle, there was Laraghbryan, an early monastic site associated with St Senan.
threads.spokenNarrative: Long before the castle, there was Laraghbryan, an early monastic site associated with St Senan. Its history reads like a run of bad luck. The death of its abbot, Glaindibur, is recorded in 767. Then its oratory was burnt and plundered by the 'men of Meath' in 1036 – and, in case the point was missed, again in 1040. It sat on a major routeway, so it may have been a rest house for pilgrims and clerics travelling east and west. A medieval service station, if you like. A medieval church still stands in the old graveyard near the Lyreen River: ivy-clad, with tall pointed windows probably from the 14th century and a later three-storied tower. By 1630 its chancel was described as 'uncovered', which sounds draughty. And one old record even says the First Earl of Kildare died here, in 1316. A quiet spot now, for somewhere with that much drama.
